sentences.text: Toretocnemus is an extinct genus of ichthyosaurs, a group of marine reptiles adapted to underwater life. The genus was established by John Campbell Merriam in 1903.
This animal was a small ichthyosaur measuring less than 2 meters in length, with some estimates suggesting both species reached only about 1 meter, making it one of the smallest known ichthyosaurs.
The skull featured very large eye sockets with narrow jugal bones forming their underside, indicating that vision was a critical sense for this creature.
Its tail possessed a weak downward bend formed by caudal centra that were longer at the top than the bottom, creating a wedge-like shape.
The coracoids of Toretocnemus zitteli are rounded, twice as long as they are wide, and lack concavities on their edges.
The shaft of the femur is narrow, but its lower end is very wide.
Toretocnemus is estimated to have not exceeded 2 meters in length, with some species reaching only 1 meter, making it one of the smallest known ichthyosaurs.
The name Leptocheirus was preoccupied, leading George Albert Boulenger to rename it Merriamia in 1904.
The genus Toretocnemus was first described in 1903 by John Campbell Merriam based on fossils found in the Hosselkus Limestone of Shasta County.
The holotype specimen UCMP 8100 was discovered along the Pit River in Shasta County, California, by Annie Montague Alexander.
Spencer Lucas noted that, unlike most taxa found in the Antimonio Formation, Toretocnemus showed a very limited geographic distribution and was not present in Nevada deposits.
Ichthyosaurs, including Toretocnemus, gave birth to live young underwater because reptile eggs would drown if laid in water.
Unlike modern poikilothermic reptiles, ichthyosaurs had high metabolisms and were homeotherms capable of maintaining a constant body temperature.
Researchers suggest that Triassic ichthyosaurs like Toretocnemus may have been ambush predators due to being less efficient swimmers than later species.
Ichthyosaurs had large eyes indicating vision was important, and their nostrils leading to mouths allowed them to scent prey underwater.
Ichthyosaurs propelled themselves forward by beating their tails back and forth, an efficient method for sustained swimming, though later studies have doubted the use of limbs for propulsion.
The front edge of the limb of T. zitteli likely had more muscle power than the rear edge due to the placement of the humerus.
Toretocnemus is the type genus of the family Toretocnemidae, which also includes Qianichthyosaurus.
In 1999, Motani recovered Toretocnemus within Euichthyosauria rather than among the shastasaurids.
Toretocnemus lived during the Carnian stage of the Upper Triassic in what is now North America, specifically from 237 to 227.3 million years ago.

Ryosuke Motani tentatively maintained both T. californicus and T. zitteli as valid species because the lack of overlapping material complicated comparisons, though he later argued that because the specimens are disarticulated and incomplete, the difference in limb length between the two species is of dubious utility.
Lucas speculated that Toretocnemus may not have been a strong open-ocean swimmer because of its small size.
Paleontologist Ryosuke Motani unified the genera Toretocnemus and Merriamia under the older name Toretocnemus due to anatomical similarities and geographic proximity.
